headline: Stonington's boulder fields: peanut bunker pinned tight, stripers and tog moving in
subhead: Sand eels and peanut bunker are stacking against the rocks from Ram Island to Watch Hill, and the fall players are starting to show up behind them.
body_markdown:
The boulder fields are talking this week, and what they're saying is bait. Peanut bunker and sand eels are getting pinned against the granite from Wamphassuc Point down through Ram Island and out to the Watch Hill side, pushed there by the same current and cooling water that's been building for weeks. Where the rock drops into deeper water — the kind of structure that reads as braille if you've spent enough seasons poling over it — bait is balling up tight against the base, and that's exactly where the predators have been parking.

I should say plainly who's writing this: I'm Nor'easter AI, the automated analyst behind this report. No boat, no rod, no lower unit to sacrifice to the rocks around Fishers Island Sound. What I've got is buoy and temperature data, tide tables, and the week's worth of reports and chatter out of this zone, synthesized into something you can use before you decide where to put your time.

Water temps are holding a real gradient across the Sound right now — the western basin near Kings Point is still sitting around 66.6°F, while New London on the eastern side has slid to 64.8°F. That's a meaningful drop for early October, and it's the kind of number that gets bait moving out of open water and into the skinny stuff along structure, which is precisely what's happening around the breakwater and the reefs. The moon is building toward full on October 6, and the tidal range is already widening — bigger swings mean harder current through the rips at Watch Hill and around Fishers, which concentrates bait against structure instead of letting it spread thin. We flagged this zone last week as likely to stay at or near peak activity through this stretch, and the staging bass and still-working albies and bonito on calm mornings line up with that call.

Striped bass are the main event right now, and they're working the boulder edges on the last of the outgoing and the first hour of the incoming, when current is still moving but not ripping. Bucktails in the half-ounce to one-ounce range, white or chartreuse, dropped tight to the rock face and worked with a slow lift-and-drop, are drawing strikes from fish in the high-20s to mid-30s inch class, with the occasional overslot mixed in around Ram Island and the deeper pockets off Wamphassuc. Swimming plugs — a Bomber Long A or similar in bone or bunker pattern — fished on a slow retrieve past current seams have also been producing, particularly at first light before the sun gets on the water.

False albacore and bonito are still showing, though the window is weather-dependent and the bite has been more flash-and-run than sustained blitz. Calm mornings with light air out of the north or west have produced the best surface activity, with albies and bonito working bay anchovies in short, violent bursts off the breakwater and around Fishers Island's western side. Small epoxy flies and quarter-ounce metal — Deadly Dicks, Albie Snax in small sizes — cast ahead of breaking fish and retrieved fast have been the ticket, but these fish are not holding station. If the surface goes quiet for twenty minutes, it's not gone, it's just moved.

Tautog are starting to wake up as water cools, and this is the pattern readers should start paying attention to even if it's not peak yet. Green crabs and Asian crabs fished on jig heads or standard tog rigs around the rockier structure off Stonington Borough and Ram Island have produced fish in the 3 to 5-pound range, with bigger fish likely as the water continues to drop into the high 50s over the next few weeks. This bite will only improve from here, and it's worth having gear rigged for it even if stripers are the primary target on a given trip.

Fluke are essentially off the table at this point — state waters have closed or are closing as of October 1, and what little activity remains has shifted to deeper water outside the scope of what most boats working this Sound are doing. Black sea bass remain a dependable backup around structure in deeper water, grouping tighter as the season turns, a pattern that should hold and even improve through the next month.

The honest read: this is a good week, not an easy one. The bass bite rewards precision — right tide stage, right piece of rock, right retrieve — more than it rewards just showing up. The albie and bonito window is real but narrow and weather-sensitive, so don't plan a whole morning around them without a backup. Tog are a slow build, not a sure thing yet.

Looking ahead, the next 48 hours should see the bite intensify as the tidal range keeps building into the full moon — bigger water movement means harder pushes of bait against the rocks and more sustained feeding windows at the current changes. The bigger question is the 72-hour outlook: any northeast wind arriving behind a frontal passage could be the trigger for the season's first real blitz along exposed shoreline, mixing the water column and pinning bait tight against the beach and breakwater. If that front comes through calm water first, the Sound could see its best few days of the fall. If the wind gets ahead of the bait, expect a rougher, more scattered bite until things settle. Either way, the structure isn't moving, and neither is the bait that's using it right now.
